Submission received: 21 December 2017 / Revised: 22 January 2018 / Accepted: 24 January 2018 / Published: 27 January 2018 Abstract : In this contribution, we study the microstructural evolution of an age-hardenable AA6082 aluminum alloy during severe plastic deformation by gradation extrusion. A novel die design allowing an interruption of processing and nondestructive billet removal was developed. A systematic study on the microstructure gradient at different points of a single billet could be performed with the help of this die. Distinct gradients were investigated using microhardness measurements and electron microscopy. Our results highlight that gradation extrusion is a powerful method to produce graded materials with partially ultrafine-grained microstructures. From the point of view of obtaining an ultrafine-grained surface layer with maximum hardness, only a small number of forming elements is needed. It was also found that large incremental deformation by too many forming elements may result in locally heterogeneous microstructures and failure near the billet surface caused by localization of deformation. Furthermore, considering economical aspects of processing, fewer forming elements are preferred since several processing parameter-related cost factors are then significantly lower. 1. Introduction Severe Plastic Deformation (SPD) processes are efficient techniques to increase a material’s strength by strain hardening and grain refinement [1,2]. Many studies have been focused on the most prominent SPD processes like equal-channel angular pressing (ECAP) [3,4,5,6], accumulative roll-bonding (ARB) [7], and high-pressure torsion (HPT) [8,9]. One of the main goals of most SPD processes is the introduction of large strains into the billet, typically with the aim of a homogeneous distribution [10,11,12,13]. In order to reduce microstructural gradients and to homogenize the billet’s properties, many SPD methods make use of repeated deformation steps [14,15,16,17] until a certain homogenization of the microstructure, as well as the corresponding mechanical properties, is achieved. Multiple passes of ECAP, for example, are often used to produce homogeneous bulk ultrafine-grained materials [18,19]. Much research has been performed in order to find optimum processing routes for multi-pass ECAP with enhanced grain refinement rates and maximum homogeneity [20,21,22]. In contrast, for some practical applications there is a need for materials that provide a distinct gradient of mechanical properties. Classical approaches to obtaining property/microstructure gradients are, e.g., shot peening of ductile materials and heat treatment methods like the case hardening of steels. There are, furthermore, many techniques of surface coating which are applicable for almost every material, but are often accompanied by the formation of substrate-coating interfaces that can be disadvantageous for certain applications. For tailoring specific gradient microstructures and mechanical properties, SPD methods have rarely been used [23,24,25,26]. In the present work, a distinct microstructural gradient is created by a heterogeneous introduction of severe plastic deformation. Based on the principle of direct extrusion processing, a novel approach of gradation extrusion has recently been developed [27,28]. This bulk forming method is basically a type of direct impact extrusion that has also been registered for patent [29]. Using several geometrical cavities in the die that act as forming elements as well as enforcing a final reduction of the diameter of the rod-shaped billets (see Figure 1), a well-defined graded microstructure with a severely deformed surface region can be generated. The forming elements are comparatively small with regards to the overall die size. They can be varied in number, size, and arrangement and they generate the specific conditions needed for severe plastic deformation. Depending on the tool design, a specific local gradient in terms of grain size near the mantle surface can be produced [30]. The forming technique requires sufficient backpressure to completely fill the cavities with the material between the forming elements. This backpressure is generated by the final diameter reduction. Another important requirement for effective grain refinement is a large induced equivalent strain. The gradation extrusion principle is therefore characterized by a stepwise generation of local plastic strain at the forming elements which is accumulated during the deformation path through the corresponding tool [28,29]. This approach has a certain potential to produce an ultrafine-grained microstructure which can extend up to a depth of several millimeters from the billet’s surface. This layer is characterized by an increased strength while the inner material exhibits a high ductility due to its coarse-grained microstructure. Since the combination of local high strength and good ductility has high relevance for many practical applications, the investigated technological approach of gradation extrusion seems promising for bridging the gap between SPD methods refining the complete volume and conventional methods that only create surface strengthening in the micrometer regime. Jun 2007, 129(3): 531-538 (8 pages) https://doi.org/10.1115/1.2716719 Published Online: January 3, 2007 Article history Received: July 10, 2006 Revised: January 3, 2007 Friction drilling uses a rotating conical tool to penetrate the workpiece and create a bushing in a single step without generating chips. This research investigates the three-dimensional (3D) finite element modeling (FEM) of large plastic strain and high-temperature work-material deformation in friction drilling. The explicit FEM code with temperature-dependent mechanical and thermal properties, as well as the adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling three FEM techniques necessary to enable the convergence of solution, is applied. An inverse method to match the measured and modeling thrust force determines a coefficient of friction of 0.7 in this study. The model is validated by comparing the thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy. The FEM results show that the peak temperature of the workpiece approaches the work-material solidus temperature. Distributions of plastic strain, temperature, stress, and deformation demonstrate the thermomechanical behavior of the workpiece and advantages of 3D FEM to study of work-material deformation in friction drilling. Introduction Nanoindentation has emerged as a versatile and widely used technique for investigating mechanical properties at small length scales, ranging from nanometres to micrometres. Its relatively straightforward experimental implementation and minimal specimen preparation requirements make it well-suited for investigating all classes of materials. High spatial resolution, both laterally and in depth, makes it extremely useful for determining mechanical properties that cannot be otherwise resolved using bulk mechanical test methods. Traditionally, nanoindentation studies have focused heavily on investigating site-specific mechanical properties, such as hardness and elastic modulus [1,2], and have been limited to quasi-static strain rates (10−5 to 10−1 s−1). However, there is tremendous scientific interest in extending it to high strain rates [[3], [4], [5], [6], [7]]. Such measurements will provide valuable insights into deformation mechanisms and enable studying potential mechanism transitions at high strain rates, that, to this date, remain poorly understood. Another key motivation for developing high strain rate testing at nano/micrometer length scales is to bridge the gap between experiments and atomistic or dislocation dynamics simulations, which typically use small volumes (nm3 to µm3) and ultrahigh strain rates (>105 s−1). Such development will overcome the challenges of characterizing microscale features, such as thin films and individual phases in materials, that are otherwise difficult to test using established macroscale techniques like Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar tests [8,9] due to size constraints. Previous efforts to extend nanoindentation to high strain rate regime have primarily relied on impact-based approaches [7,[10], [11], [12], [13], [14]], in which the indenter is rapidly accelerated towards the sample for a high rate loading event. In these tests, the change in kinetic energy of the indenter, before and after the impact, is used to calculate the impact hardness of the material. While this method allows reaching higher strain rates, it offers little control over the loading profile. Upon contact, the indenter decelerates, causing the indentation strain rate to decrease with depth. This rate of decrease is material property dependent, producing distinct profiles for different materials. As a result, only a representative strain rate and a representative hardness can be extracted from such tests. Recently, laser induced particle impact test (LIPIT) has emerged as a comparable technique to nanoindentation-based impact tests, allowing the achievement of even higher strain rates [15,16]. In this method, the material surface is bombarded with particles, often using a thermal spray equipment, and a high-speed camera to capture the incoming and outgoing particle velocities. Hassani et al. [15] and Borasi et al. [16] demonstrated strain rates exceeding 106 s−1 on iron (Fe), copper (Cu) and nickel (Ni) using the LIPIT and have reported a distinct transition in the deformation behaviour at strain rates beyond 105 s−1, which was attributed to dislocation drag effects. However, LIPIT suffers from the same problems as nanoindentation impact tests: strain rate variation throughout the testing. Consequently, while impact-based methods are invaluable for exploring material behaviour under extreme dynamic conditions, they are less suited for investigations requiring controlled constant strain rates. An alternative approach, particularly desirable for systematic studies, is the use of constant strain rate (CSR) nanoindentation, during which the penetration rate is actively adjusted so that the indentation strain rate remains constant with depth. For pyramidal tips, such as Berkovich and cube-corner, CSR profiles can be achieved by maintaining the ratio of ḣ/h constant, where ḣ is the indenter tip penetration rate and h is the instantaneous displacement [17]. Since the indenter penetration rate increases proportionately with depth, they are also termed as “proportional profiles”. For other indenter tip shapes, such as spherical tips, analogous functions can be used [18]. The successful application of CSR profiles by Maier et al. [19,20] and others have demonstrated the utility of CSR profiles in accurately determining strain rate sensitivity of materials using indentation. Results obtained with CSR profiles in nanoindentation have shown excellent agreement with micropillar compression [18,20] and bulk tensile tests [19] for extracting reliable strain rate sensitivity exponents, underscoring the robustness of this approach. Typically, CSR loading profiles are implemented using a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) feedback loop that regulates the input signal (voltage or current) to maintain the target variable (load or depth) at the desired rate. Merle et al. [6] demonstrated that the PID feedback loop on a load-controlled nanoindenter could achieve CSR profiles up to 102 s−1. However, at strain rates of 103 s−1, the 1 kHz PID loop was found to be insufficient, leading to large fluctuations in indentation strain rate. Guillonneau et al. [5] and Cherukuri et al. [21] reported CSR nanoindentation tests up to 103 s−1 using an intrinsically displacement-controlled indenter and by applying the input voltages directly, without using the PID feedback loop. However, the methodology used to achieve the highest indentation strain rates have not been described adequately. Overall, CSR nanoindentation tests seem to remain mostly limited to 103 s−1 [5,21]. Extending CSR nanoindentation to high strain rates requires significant improvements in instrumentation, testing protocols and data analysis methods [6,10,21]. Branch report on tool-material interaction and heat/pressure effects

Friction drilling is fundamentally a contact-based process where tool-workpiece interaction generates both heat and pressure, which strongly influence deformation and material behavior. The process relies on the heat generated from the frictional force between the tool and sheet metal workpiece to soften, penetrate, and deform the workpiece [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The tool wear mechanisms in friction drilling are categorized into abrasive wear, adhesive wear, and oxidative wear [N3-R1]. These contact effects are not passive; they actively shape the deformation path by changing the frictional resistance and the heat generation profile during drilling.

The frictional heating and contact pressure in friction drilling are directly tied to the thermomechanical response of the material. The explicit finite element method (FEM) used in friction drilling modeling accounts for large plastic strain, large plastic deformation, and high-temperature work-material deformation, with adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence [N4-F3]. This highlights that the process simultaneously generates high temperatures and localized plastic deformation, and that the resulting thermomechanical state cannot be separated from the contact mechanics. The study also reports that the peak temperature of the workpiece approaches the work-material solidus temperature [N4-F3], underscoring the extreme thermal conditions that can arise during friction drilling.

Tool wear and heat generation together alter material deformation behavior. Tool wear mechanisms—abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative—change how the tool interacts with the workpiece, affecting the force transmission, friction coefficient, and hence the localized heating and plastic deformation [N3-R1]. The inverse method used in thermo-mechanical finite element modeling of friction drilling matches measured and modeled thrust force to determine a coefficient of friction of 0.7 in that study [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. This implies that wear-induced changes in friction behavior are not just experimental artifacts; they are meaningful deformation drivers that must be incorporated into process analysis. The model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy [N4-F3], showing that friction drilling is a highly coupled thermomechanical process where contact effects are central to the deformation response.

Material removal or softening further complicates property determination. The friction drilling process is described as relying on heat generation to soften the workpiece and allow penetration and deformation [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This means that the material is not simply being cut in the traditional sense; it is being softened locally, which can lead to non-uniform deformation behavior and make it difficult to separate true material response from process-induced softening. The tool-workpiece interaction also generates localized subsurface effects, as friction drilling changes workpiece microstructure and material properties due to high strain and temperature [N3-R3][N3-R5]. Because the material is being softened and deformed by localized heating and friction, the measured properties may reflect a mixture of the intrinsic material behavior and the process-induced state, making direct determination of the material’s intrinsic physical properties challenging.

Overall, the main challenges in tool-material interaction are the coupling of heat, pressure, wear, and friction into a single thermomechanical response; the difficulty of isolating material behavior from process effects; and the need for models that can capture both contact mechanics and deformation evolution simultaneously. The evidence supports a view of friction drilling as a highly nonlinear process where contact effects are not just boundary conditions but active contributors to the deformation state and residual property distribution [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N4-F3].

Branch report on measurement and instrumentation challenges

During friction drilling, the most difficult measurement signals to capture are those that are transient, localized, and highly coupled with the thermomechanical response of the material. The process involves high-speed deformation, rapid heat generation, and large plastic strain, which means that the signals of interest—such as strain, force, torque, temperature, and microstructural state—are not static but evolve rapidly during the process [N1-R3][N1-R5][N5-F4]. The cited nanoindentation study on constant strain rate testing emphasizes that high strain rate measurements are experimentally challenging because they require careful control of the rate profile and accurate capture of dynamic responses [N5-F4]. This same principle applies to friction drilling, where the strain rate and temperature field can change dramatically over the course of the operation.

Strain rate and temperature strongly affect sensor accuracy and response. Strain gauges and other sensors may distort rapid force inputs and are sensitive to natural frequency effects [N5-R2]. High-frequency sampling is recommended to capture accurate waveforms and peak strain values, with rates 10–20× higher than the highest frequency of interest [N5-R4]. This is particularly relevant in friction drilling because the process can produce large plastic strain, high temperature, and high-frequency dynamic loading that sensors may not resolve if their sampling rate is insufficient [N5-F4]. The evidence also indicates that sensor response can be inadequate at higher strain rates: for example, a 1 kHz PID loop was found to be insufficient at strain rates of 103 s−1, leading to large fluctuations in indentation strain rate [N5-F4]. In friction drilling, where the process is inherently high-strain-rate and high-temperature, the same limitations likely apply to strain and force measurements.

The limitations of existing instrumentation for in-process monitoring are substantial. The cited friction drilling dissertation reports that experimental analysis of the process involves thrust force and torque measurements, and that thermal finite element modeling is used to predict temperature [N2-F2]. It also notes that details of microstructure and material property changes remain difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5]. This points to a broader problem: even when instrumentation is available, it may not be sufficient to resolve the full range of relevant signals. The explicit FEM study for friction drilling explicitly uses adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence, which suggests that the process is computationally intensive and may require specialized monitoring approaches [N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that inverse methods are used to match measured and modeled thrust force, but this also implies that the data required for inverse calibration may be incomplete or noisy [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].

In-process monitoring is further constrained by the need for both high temporal resolution and spatial resolution. Nanoindentation-based methods show that strain rate control is difficult at higher rates, and that impact-based methods produce variable strain rates with depth rather than constant profiles [N5-F4]. This is relevant because friction drilling may involve localized deformation and subsurface changes that are hard to observe in real time. The cited evidence also highlights that experimental considerations for high-strain-rate nanoindentation require careful calibrations and data analysis for reliable hardness measurements [N5-F4]. Translating this into friction drilling, it means that existing instrumentation may capture only part of the process, and that the remaining parts—such as localized subsurface deformation, microstructure evolution, and transient temperature changes—remain under-resolved.

Overall, the measurement and instrumentation challenges in friction drilling are severe because the process combines high strain rate, high temperature, and dynamic contact effects. Sensors must operate at high frequency, resist distortion, and capture transient responses, yet current instrumentation often struggles to do so reliably. The evidence supports the conclusion that in-process monitoring is limited by both the physical nature of the process and the practical constraints of existing sensors, making direct and reliable determination of material properties during friction drilling difficult [N1-R3][N1-R5][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-F4].

Branch report on modeling and data integration challenges

The main gaps between experimental data and predictive models in friction drilling are the mismatch between observed process behavior and the assumptions embedded in the model. The thermo-mechanical finite element modeling study explicitly states that the model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy [N4-F3]. This is a strong validation statement, but it also implies a gap: the model captures some observable quantities well, yet it still requires inverse methods to estimate parameters such as the coefficient of friction [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. This gap suggests that experimental data are not sufficient on their own to fully parameterize the model, and that model predictions depend on calibration against limited process outputs.

A major need for data fusion or multi-scale modeling arises because friction drilling involves both macroscopic and microscopic effects. The process is described as producing large plastic strain, large plastic deformation, and high-temperature work-material deformation, and the explicit FEM study uses adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence [N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that microstructure evolution and residual stress are important outcomes of the process [N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R3]. This means that a single-scale model may miss the coupling between macroscopic thermomechanical behavior and microscopic microstructural evolution. The cited friction drilling dissertation also reports that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature, yet details of these changes are difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5]. This suggests a clear need for multi-scale modeling that integrates process-level thermomechanical analysis with microstructure evolution and residual stress prediction [N4-F3][N3-R3][N6-R3].

Limitations of inverse methods and calibration are evident in the friction drilling literature. The inverse method used in thermo-mechanical finite element modeling determines a coefficient of friction of 0.7 by matching measured and modeled thrust force [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. While this is a useful calibration approach, it also shows that the inverse method depends heavily on the quality and representativeness of the experimental data. If the measured signals are incomplete, noisy, or biased by process effects such as tool wear or localized softening, the resulting calibration may not generalize well [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The same study also reports that the model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements, but the evidence does not indicate whether all relevant process variables are captured [N4-F3]. This implies a calibration limitation: the model may be tuned to some observable outputs, but it may still underpredict or misrepresent other important quantities.

The cited constant strain rate nanoindentation study reinforces the broader limitation of inverse methods in high-strain-rate processes. It shows that impact-based methods produce variable strain rates with depth, making it difficult to extract representative material properties [N5-F4]. This is directly relevant to friction drilling, where the process is itself a high-strain-rate, high-temperature deformation event and where the measured output may reflect a mixture of material response and process-induced softening [N3-R3][N3-R5]. In that context, inverse methods may become overly dependent on the selected calibration targets and may fail to account for the true underlying deformation mechanism.

Overall, the modeling and data integration challenges in friction drilling are centered on the gap between experimental data and predictive models, the need for multi-scale data fusion, and the limitations of inverse calibration. The evidence supports a view that friction drilling is a highly coupled process where process data alone are insufficient for full model parameterization, and that better integration of thermomechanical, microstructural, and residual stress data is needed to improve predictive accuracy [N4-F3][N3-R3][N6-R3][N5-F4].

Branch report on material property changes under severe plastic deformation

Severe plastic deformation in friction drilling alters material properties through work hardening and microstructural evolution. The cited friction drilling dissertation explicitly states that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature, and that details of these changes are difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5]. The same source also links the process to microstructural alterations associated with friction drilling of steel, aluminum, and titanium [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This indicates that friction drilling is a form of severe plastic deformation that can induce significant microstructural transformation, even though the exact nature of those transformations may remain poorly resolved in experimental observation [N3-R5].

Work hardening and microstructural evolution are the primary mechanisms by which material properties change. The gradation extrusion study on severe plastic deformation reports that work hardening and grain refinement during local severe plastic deformation led to a considerable increase in hardness [N2-R1]. It also states that large incremental deformation by too many forming elements may result in locally heterogeneous microstructures and failure near the billet surface caused by localization of deformation [N2-F1]. This is directly relevant to friction drilling because the process also involves localized severe plastic deformation and can produce heterogeneous microstructures. The microstructural evolution study on severe plastic deformation by gradation extrusion further highlights that a systematic study of microstructure gradients could be performed, with distinct gradients investigated using microhardness measurements and electron microscopy [N2-F1]. This supports the conclusion that friction drilling, like other severe plastic deformation processes, can produce a gradient in material properties and microstructure rather than uniform strengthening.

Residual stresses and localized deformation affect property uniformity. The friction drilling dissertation notes that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature [N3-R3][N3-R5], and that tool wear mechanisms are categorized into abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative wear [N3-R1]. These effects are likely to produce localized changes in the deformation state and residual stress state. The residual stress literature cited here also states that local friction conditions are the primary cause of substantial surface residual stress [N6-R2], and that residual stresses resulting from thermo-mechanical processing can cause in-process cracking, machining distortion, in-service distortion, and/or cracking [N6-R4]. This means that friction drilling does not just change the bulk material; it can also generate significant residual stress fields that alter the mechanical response and uniformity of the material.

Differences between bulk and surface property behavior are clear in friction drilling. The friction drilling process is described as relying on heat generation to soften, penetrate, and deform the workpiece [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This suggests that surface and subsurface layers may experience different deformation histories, temperatures, and strain rates compared to the bulk. The subsurface microstructure evolution and residual stress literature explicitly investigates the effect of cutting on microstructure and subsurface properties of a cut specimen [N6-R5]. This is directly relevant because friction drilling can generate localized subsurface effects that are distinct from the bulk material. The evidence also indicates that work hardening and grain refinement can produce a considerable increase in hardness [N2-R1], while localized deformation can lead to heterogeneous microstructures and failure near the billet surface [N2-F1]. Together, these findings show that friction drilling can produce a surface-dominated strengthening response alongside a bulk-dominated deformation response, with the subsurface acting as an intermediate layer where residual stresses and microstructural gradients accumulate [N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Overall, the material property changes under severe plastic deformation in friction drilling are dominated by work hardening and microstructural evolution, but these changes are strongly coupled with residual stresses and localized deformation. The evidence supports the conclusion that friction drilling produces heterogeneous material behavior, with surface and subsurface properties often differing from the bulk and with residual stress fields that can further alter uniformity and mechanical response [N2-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R2][N6-R5].

The same source also links the process to microstructural alterations associated with friction drilling of steel, aluminum, and titanium [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This indicates that friction drilling is a form of severe plastic deformation that can induce significant microstructural transformation, even though the exact nature of those transformations may remain poorly resolved in experimental observation [N3-R5].

Work hardening and microstructural evolution are the primary mechanisms by which material properties change. The gradation extrusion study on severe plastic deformation reports that work hardening and grain refinement during local severe plastic deformation led to a considerable increase in hardness [N2-R1]. It also states that large incremental deformation by too many forming elements may result in locally heterogeneous microstructures and failure near the billet surface caused by localization of deformation [N2-F1]. This is directly relevant to friction drilling because the process also involves localized severe plastic deformation and can produce heterogeneous microstructures. The evidence further supports the conclusion that friction drilling can produce a gradient in material properties and microstructure rather than uniform strengthening [N2-R1][N2-F1].

## 5) Tool-workpiece contact and heat/pressure effects alter deformation behavior
Friction drilling is fundamentally a contact-based process where tool-workpiece interaction generates both heat and pressure. The process relies on the heat generated from the frictional force between the tool and sheet metal workpiece to soften, penetrate, and deform the workpiece [N3-R2][N3-R5]. Tool wear mechanisms are categorized into abrasive wear, adhesive wear, and oxidative wear [N3-R1]. These contact effects are not passive; they actively shape the deformation path by changing the frictional resistance and the heat generation profile during drilling.

The frictional heating and contact pressure in friction drilling are directly tied to the thermomechanical response of the material. The explicit finite element method (FEM) used in friction drilling modeling accounts for large plastic strain, large plastic deformation, and high-temperature work-material deformation, with adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence [N4-F3]. This highlights that the process simultaneously generates high temperatures and localized plastic deformation, and that the resulting thermomechanical state cannot be separated from the contact mechanics. The study also reports that the peak temperature of the workpiece approaches the work-material solidus temperature [N4-F3], underscoring the extreme thermal conditions that can arise during friction drilling.

Tool wear and heat generation together alter material deformation behavior. Tool wear mechanisms—abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative—change how the tool interacts with the workpiece, affecting the force transmission, friction coefficient, and hence the localized heating and plastic deformation [N3-R1]. The inverse method used in thermo-mechanical finite element modeling of friction drilling matches measured and modeled thrust force to determine a coefficient of friction of 0.7 in that study [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. This implies that wear-induced changes in friction behavior are not just experimental artifacts; they are meaningful deformation drivers that must be incorporated into process analysis. The model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy [N4-F3], showing that friction drilling is a highly coupled thermomechanical process where contact effects are central to the deformation response.

## 6) Material removal or softening can distort property determination
Material removal or softening further complicates property determination. The friction drilling process is described as relying on heat generation to soften the workpiece and allow penetration and deformation [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This means that the material is not simply being cut in the traditional sense; it is being softened locally, which can lead to non-uniform deformation behavior and make it difficult to separate true material response from process-induced softening.

The tool-workpiece interaction also generates localized subsurface effects, as friction drilling changes workpiece microstructure and material properties due to high strain and temperature [N3-R3][N3-R5]. Because the material is being softened and deformed by localized heating and friction, the measured properties may reflect a mixture of the intrinsic material behavior and the process-induced state, making direct determination of the material’s intrinsic physical properties challenging [N3-R3][N3-R5].

## 7) Residual stresses and localized deformation affect property uniformity
Residual stresses and localized deformation affect property uniformity. The friction drilling dissertation notes that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature [N3-R3][N3-R5], and that tool wear mechanisms are categorized into abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative wear [N3-R1]. These effects are likely to produce localized changes in the deformation state and residual stress state.

The residual stress literature cited here also states that local friction conditions are the primary cause of substantial surface residual stress [N6-R2], and that residual stresses resulting from thermo-mechanical processing can cause in-process cracking, machining distortion, in-service distortion, and/or cracking [N6-R4]. This means that friction drilling does not just change the bulk material; it can also generate significant residual stress fields that alter the mechanical response and uniformity of the material.

## 8) Surface and bulk property behavior can differ significantly
The difference between bulk and surface property behavior is especially important in friction drilling. The process relies on heat generation to soften, penetrate, and deform the workpiece [N3-R2][N3-R5], which suggests that surface and subsurface layers may experience different deformation histories, temperatures, and strain rates compared to the bulk. The subsurface microstructure evolution and residual stress literature explicitly investigates the effect of cutting on microstructure and subsurface properties of a cut specimen [N6-R5]. This is directly relevant because friction drilling can generate localized subsurface effects that are distinct from the bulk material.

The evidence also indicates that work hardening and grain refinement can produce a considerable increase in hardness [N2-R1], while localized deformation can lead to heterogeneous microstructures and failure near the billet surface [N2-F1]. Together, these findings show that friction drilling can produce a surface-dominated strengthening response alongside a bulk-dominated deformation response, with the subsurface acting as an intermediate layer where residual stresses and microstructural gradients accumulate [N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R5].

## 9) Modeling and data integration are limited by gaps and calibration dependence
The main gaps between experimental data and predictive models are the mismatch between observed process behavior and the assumptions embedded in the model. The thermo-mechanical finite element modeling study explicitly states that the model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy [N4-F3]. This is a strong validation statement, but it also implies a gap: the model captures some observable quantities well, yet it still requires inverse methods to estimate parameters such as the coefficient of friction [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. This gap suggests that experimental data are not sufficient on their own to fully parameterize the model, and that model predictions depend on calibration against limited process outputs.

A major need for data fusion or multi-scale modeling arises because friction drilling involves both macroscopic and microscopic effects. The process is described as producing large plastic strain, large plastic deformation, and high-temperature work-material deformation, and the explicit FEM study uses adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence [N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that microstructure evolution and residual stress are important outcomes of the process [N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R3]. This means that a single-scale model may miss the coupling between macroscopic thermomechanical behavior and microscopic microstructural evolution. The cited friction drilling dissertation also reports that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature, yet details of these changes are difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5]. This suggests a clear need for multi-scale modeling that integrates process-level thermomechanical analysis with microstructure evolution and residual stress prediction [N4-F3][N3-R3][N6-R3].

Limitations of inverse methods and calibration are evident in the friction drilling literature. The inverse method used in thermo-mechanical finite element modeling determines a coefficient of friction of 0.7 by matching measured and modeled thrust force [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. While this is a useful calibration approach, it also shows that the inverse method depends heavily on the quality and representativeness of the experimental data. If the measured signals are incomplete, noisy, or biased by process effects such as tool wear or localized softening, the resulting calibration may not generalize well [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The same study also reports that the model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements, but the evidence does not indicate whether all relevant process variables are captured [N4-F3]. This implies a calibration limitation: the model may be tuned to some observable outputs, but it may still underpredict or misrepresent other important quantities.

The cited constant strain rate nanoindentation study reinforces the broader limitation of inverse methods in high-strain-rate processes. It shows that impact-based methods produce variable strain rates with depth, making it difficult to extract representative material properties [N5-F4]. This is directly relevant to friction drilling, where the process is itself a high-strain-rate, high-temperature deformation event and where the measured output may reflect a mixture of material response and process-induced softening [N3-R3][N3-R5]. In that context, inverse methods may become overly dependent on the selected calibration targets and may fail to account for the true underlying deformation mechanism.

## 10) Overall conclusion
The main challenges of determining the physical properties of materials during severe plastic deformation in friction drilling are therefore:

- **Measurement difficulty**: Transient, localized, and coupled signals are hard to capture in real time.
- **Sensor limitations**: Strain rate and temperature affect sensor accuracy and response; high-frequency sampling is needed, but current instrumentation may still be inadequate.
- **In-process monitoring limits**: Even when instrumentation exists, it may not resolve the full range of relevant signals.
- **Material property changes**: Work hardening, microstructural evolution, and residual stresses alter the material state.
- **Localized and surface-bulk mismatch**: Surface and subsurface properties often differ from the bulk, and residual stress fields can reduce uniformity.
- **Tool-contact effects**: Friction, heat, pressure, and tool wear actively shape the deformation response.
- **Modeling and calibration gaps**: Experimental data do not fully parameterize predictive models, and inverse methods depend heavily on calibration quality.

Taken together, these challenges mean that determining the true physical properties of materials during friction drilling is not straightforward. The process itself is a highly coupled thermomechanical event in which measurement, deformation, and modeling are tightly intertwined, and accurate property determination requires both better instrumentation and more comprehensive integration of process, microstructure, and residual stress data [N3-R3][N3-R5][N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N5-F4][N6-R2][N6-R4].

During friction drilling, the most difficult measurement signals to capture are those that are transient, localized, and highly coupled with the thermomechanical response of the material. The process involves high-speed deformation, rapid heat generation, and large plastic strain, which means that the signals of interest—such as strain, force, torque, temperature, and microstructural state—are not static but evolve rapidly during the process [N1-R3][N1-R5][N5-F4]. The cited nanoindentation study on constant strain rate testing emphasizes that high strain rate measurements are experimentally challenging because they require careful control of the rate profile and accurate capture of dynamic responses [N5-F4]. This same principle applies to friction drilling, where the strain rate and temperature field can change dramatically over the course of the operation.

Strain rate and temperature strongly affect sensor accuracy and response. Strain gauges and other sensors may distort rapid force inputs and are sensitive to natural frequency effects [N5-R2]. High-frequency sampling is recommended to capture accurate waveforms and peak strain values, with rates 10–20× higher than the highest frequency of interest [N5-R4]. This is particularly relevant in friction drilling because the process can produce large plastic strain, high temperature, and high-frequency dynamic loading that sensors may not resolve if their sampling rate is insufficient [N5-F4]. The evidence also indicates that sensor response can be inadequate at higher strain rates: for example, a 1 kHz PID loop was found to be insufficient at strain rates of 103 s−1, leading to large fluctuations in indentation strain rate [N5-F4]. In friction drilling, where the process is inherently high-strain-rate and high-temperature, the same limitations likely apply to strain and force measurements.

The limitations of existing instrumentation for in-process monitoring are substantial. The cited friction drilling dissertation reports that experimental analysis of the process involves thrust force and torque measurements, and that thermal finite element modeling is used to predict temperature [N2-F2]. It also notes that details of microstructure and material property changes remain difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5]. This points to a broader problem: even when instrumentation is available, it may not be sufficient to resolve the full range of relevant signals. The explicit FEM study for friction drilling explicitly uses adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence, which suggests that the process is computationally intensive and may require specialized monitoring approaches [N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that inverse methods are used to match measured and modeled thrust force, but this also implies that the data required for inverse calibration may be incomplete or noisy [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].

Branch report on tool-material interaction and heat/pressure effects

Friction drilling is fundamentally a contact-based process where tool-workpiece interaction generates both heat and pressure, which strongly influence deformation and material behavior. The process relies on the heat generated from the frictional force between the tool and sheet metal workpiece to soften, penetrate, and deform the workpiece [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The tool wear mechanisms in friction drilling are categorized into abrasive wear, adhesive wear, and oxidative wear [N3-R1]. These contact effects are not passive; they actively shape the deformation path by changing the frictional resistance and the heat generation profile during drilling.

The frictional heating and contact pressure in friction drilling are directly tied to the thermomechanical response of the material. The explicit finite element method (FEM) used in friction drilling modeling accounts for large plastic strain, large plastic deformation, and high-temperature work-material deformation, with adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence [N4-F3]. This highlights that the process simultaneously generates high temperatures and localized plastic deformation, and that the resulting thermomechanical state cannot be separated from the contact mechanics. The study also reports that the peak temperature of the workpiece approaches the work-material solidus temperature [N4-F3], underscoring the extreme thermal conditions that can arise during friction drilling.

Tool wear and heat generation together alter material deformation behavior. Tool wear mechanisms—abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative—change how the tool interacts with the workpiece, affecting the force transmission, friction coefficient, and hence the localized heating and plastic deformation [N3-R1]. The inverse method used in thermo-mechanical finite element modeling of friction drilling matches measured and modeled thrust force to determine a coefficient of friction of 0.7 in that study [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. This implies that wear-induced changes in friction behavior are not just experimental artifacts; they are meaningful deformation drivers that must be incorporated into process analysis. The model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy [N4-F3], showing that friction drilling is a highly coupled thermomechanical process where contact effects are central to the deformation response.

Material removal or softening further complicates property determination. The friction drilling process is described as relying on heat generation to soften the workpiece and allow penetration and deformation [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This means that the material is not simply being cut in the traditional sense; it is being softened locally, which can lead to non-uniform deformation behavior and make it difficult to separate true material response from process-induced softening. The tool-workpiece interaction also generates localized subsurface effects, as friction drilling changes workpiece microstructure and material properties due to high strain and temperature [N3-R3][N3-R5]. Because the material is being softened and deformed by localized heating and friction, the measured properties may reflect a mixture of the intrinsic material behavior and the process-induced state, making direct determination of the material’s intrinsic physical properties challenging.

Overall, the main challenges in tool-material interaction are the coupling of heat, pressure, wear, and friction into a single thermomechanical response; the difficulty of isolating material behavior from process effects; and the need for models that can capture both contact mechanics and deformation evolution simultaneously. The evidence supports a view of friction drilling as a highly nonlinear process where contact effects are not just boundary conditions but active contributors to the deformation state and residual property distribution [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N4-F3].

During friction drilling, the most difficult measurement signals to capture are those that are transient, localized, and highly coupled with the thermomechanical response of the material. The process involves high-speed deformation, rapid heat generation, and large plastic strain, which means that the signals of interest—such as strain, force, torque, temperature, and microstructural state—are not static but evolve rapidly during the process [N1-R3][N1-R5][N5-F4]. The cited nanoindentation study on constant strain rate testing emphasizes that high strain rate measurements are experimentally challenging because they require careful control of the rate profile and accurate capture of dynamic responses [N5-F4]. This same principle applies to friction drilling, where the strain rate and temperature field can change dramatically over the course of the operation.

Strain rate and temperature strongly affect sensor accuracy and response. Strain gauges and other sensors may distort rapid force inputs and are sensitive to natural frequency effects [N5-R2]. High-frequency sampling is recommended to capture accurate waveforms and peak strain values, with rates 10–20× higher than the highest frequency of interest [N5-R4]. This is particularly relevant in friction drilling because the process can produce large plastic strain, high temperature, and high-frequency dynamic loading that sensors may not resolve if their sampling rate is insufficient [N5-F4]. The evidence also indicates that sensor response can be inadequate at higher strain rates: for example, a 1 kHz PID loop was found to be insufficient at strain rates of 103 s−1, leading to large fluctuations in indentation strain rate [N5-F4]. In friction drilling, where the process is inherently high-strain-rate and high-temperature, the same limitations likely apply to strain and force measurements.

The limitations of existing instrumentation for in-process monitoring are substantial. The cited friction drilling dissertation reports that experimental analysis of the process involves thrust force and torque measurements, and that thermal finite element modeling is used to predict temperature [N2-F2]. It also notes that details of microstructure and material property changes remain difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5]. This points to a broader problem: even when instrumentation is available, it may not be sufficient to resolve the full range of relevant signals. The explicit FEM study for friction drilling explicitly uses adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence, which suggests that the process is computationally intensive and may require specialized monitoring approaches [N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that inverse methods are used to match measured and modeled thrust force, but this also implies that the data required for inverse calibration may be incomplete or noisy [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].

In-process monitoring is further constrained by the need for both high temporal resolution and spatial resolution. Nanoindentation-based methods show that strain rate control is difficult at higher rates, and that impact-based methods produce variable strain rates with depth rather than constant profiles [N5-F4]. Translating this into friction drilling, it means that existing instrumentation may capture only part of the process, and that the remaining parts—such as localized subsurface deformation, microstructure evolution, and transient temperature changes—remain under-resolved.

Overall, the measurement and instrumentation challenges in friction drilling are severe because the process combines high strain rate, high temperature, and dynamic contact effects. Sensors must operate at high frequency, resist distortion, and capture transient responses, yet current instrumentation often struggles to do so reliably. The thermo-mechanical finite element modeling study explicitly states that the model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy [N4-F3]. This is a strong validation statement, but it also implies a gap: the model captures some observable quantities well, yet it still requires inverse methods to estimate parameters such as the coefficient of friction [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. This gap suggests that experimental data are not sufficient on their own to fully parameterize the model, and that model predictions depend on calibration against limited process outputs.

A major need for data fusion or multi-scale modeling arises because friction drilling involves both macroscopic and microscopic effects. The process is described as producing large plastic strain, large plastic deformation, and high-temperature work-material deformation, and the explicit FEM study uses adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence [N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that microstructure evolution and residual stress are important outcomes of the process [N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R3]. This means that a single-scale model may miss the coupling between macroscopic thermomechanical behavior and microscopic microstructural evolution. The cited friction drilling dissertation also reports that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature, yet details of these changes are difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5]. This suggests a clear need for multi-scale modeling that integrates process-level thermomechanical analysis with microstructure evolution and residual stress prediction [N4-F3][N3-R3][N6-R3].

Limitations of inverse methods and calibration are evident in the friction drilling literature. The inverse method used in thermo-mechanical finite element modeling determines a coefficient of friction of 0.7 by matching measured and modeled thrust force [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. While this is a useful calibration approach, it also shows that the inverse method depends heavily on the quality and representativeness of the experimental data. If the measured signals are incomplete, noisy, or biased by process effects such as tool wear or localized softening, the resulting calibration may not generalize well [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The same study also reports that the model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements, but the evidence does not indicate whether all relevant process variables are captured [N4-F3]. This implies a calibration limitation: the model may be tuned to some observable outputs, but it may still underpredict or misrepresent other important quantities.

The cited constant strain rate nanoindentation study reinforces the broader limitation of inverse methods in high-strain-rate processes. It shows that impact-based methods produce variable strain rates with depth, making it difficult to extract representative material properties [N5-F4]. Work hardening and microstructural evolution are the primary mechanisms by which material properties change. The gradation extrusion study on severe plastic deformation reports that work hardening and grain refinement during local severe plastic deformation led to a considerable increase in hardness [N2-R1]. It also states that large incremental deformation by too many forming elements may result in locally heterogeneous microstructures and failure near the billet surface caused by localization of deformation [N2-F1]. This is directly relevant to friction drilling because the process also involves localized severe plastic deformation and can produce heterogeneous microstructures. The microstructural evolution study on severe plastic deformation by gradation extrusion further highlights that a systematic study of microstructure gradients could be performed, with distinct gradients investigated using microhardness measurements and electron microscopy [N2-F1]. This supports the conclusion that friction drilling, like other severe plastic deformation processes, can produce a gradient in material properties and microstructure rather than uniform strengthening.

Residual stresses and localized deformation affect property uniformity. The friction drilling dissertation notes that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature [N3-R3][N3-R5], and that tool wear mechanisms are categorized into abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative wear [N3-R1]. These effects are likely to produce localized changes in the deformation state and residual stress state. The residual stress literature cited here also states that local friction conditions are the primary cause of substantial surface residual stress [N6-R2], and that residual stresses resulting from thermo-mechanical processing can cause in-process cracking, machining distortion, in-service distortion, and/or cracking [N6-R4]. This means that friction drilling does not just change the bulk material; it can also generate significant residual stress fields that alter the mechanical response and uniformity of the material.

Differences between bulk and surface property behavior are clear in friction drilling. The friction drilling process is described as relying on heat generation to soften, penetrate, and deform the workpiece [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This suggests that surface and subsurface layers may experience different deformation histories, temperatures, and strain rates compared to the bulk. The subsurface microstructure evolution and residual stress literature explicitly investigates the effect of cutting on microstructure and subsurface properties of a cut specimen [N6-R5]. This is directly relevant because friction drilling can generate localized subsurface effects that are distinct from the bulk material. The evidence also indicates that work hardening and grain refinement can produce a considerable increase in hardness [N2-R1], while localized deformation can lead to heterogeneous microstructures and failure near the billet surface [N2-F1]. Together, these findings show that friction drilling can produce a surface-dominated strengthening response alongside a bulk-dominated deformation response, with the subsurface acting as an intermediate layer where residual stresses and microstructural gradients accumulate [N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Overall, the material property changes under severe plastic deformation in friction drilling are dominated by work hardening and microstructural evolution, but these changes are strongly coupled with residual stresses and localized deformation. The evidence supports the conclusion that friction drilling produces heterogeneous material behavior, with surface and subsurface properties often differing from the bulk and with residual stress fields that can further alter uniformity and mechanical response [N2-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Integrated final answer on the main challenges of determining physical properties during severe plastic deformation in friction drilling

Determining the physical properties of materials during severe plastic deformation in friction drilling is challenging because the process combines high-speed deformation, intense heat generation, tool-workpiece contact effects, and microstructural evolution. These factors make it difficult to separate intrinsic material behavior from process-induced changes, and they also place severe demands on measurement, modeling, and data integration. Below, I synthesize the four branch reports into a coherent explanation of the main challenges.

## 1) The process itself makes measurement difficult
Friction drilling is inherently a highly dynamic process in which transient, localized, and strongly coupled signals are hard to capture. The friction drilling dissertation notes that the process involves thrust force, torque, and thermal finite element modeling of temperature, while also stating that details of microstructure and material property changes remain difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5][N2-F2]. This means that the most important signals for determining physical properties are often not fully observable in real time.

The high-strain-rate nature of the process is especially problematic. Strain gauges and other sensors may distort rapid force inputs and are sensitive to natural frequency effects [N5-R2]. High-frequency sampling is needed to capture accurate waveforms and peak strain values, with sampling rates 10–20× higher than the highest frequency of interest [N5-R4]. In friction drilling, where large plastic strain, high temperature, and dynamic contact effects are common, the same limitations likely apply to strain and force measurements [N1-R3][N1-R5][N5-F4].

Temperature is another difficult signal. The friction drilling process relies on heat generated from frictional force between the tool and workpiece, and the peak temperature of the workpiece can approach the work-material solidus temperature [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This means that temperature measurements must operate in a regime where rapid thermal transients and extreme local heating are common, which is not trivial for in-process monitoring [N4-F3].

## 2) Strain rate and temperature affect sensor accuracy and response
Strain rate and temperature strongly affect sensor accuracy and response. The evidence shows that sensor response can be inadequate at higher strain rates: for example, a 1 kHz PID loop was found to be insufficient at strain rates of 10³ s⁻¹, leading to large fluctuations in indentation strain rate [N5-F4]. In friction drilling, where the process can produce high strain rate deformation and localized high-temperature conditions, sensors may not resolve the true signal if their sampling frequency or response characteristics are not adequate [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-F4].

Temperature also affects measurement reliability. The friction drilling dissertation explicitly uses thermal finite element modeling to predict temperature [N2-F2], which indicates that temperature is not just an output of interest but a critical process variable that must be measured and modeled. The explicit finite element study for friction drilling further notes that the model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy [N4-F3]. This implies that temperature is a necessary part of the process-state description, but that it is also hard to measure reliably in real time during severe plastic deformation.

## 3) Existing instrumentation has limitations for in-process monitoring
The instrumentation available for in-process monitoring is limited in several ways. The friction drilling literature shows that experimental analysis of the process involves thrust force and torque measurements, but the details of microstructure and material property changes are still difficult to capture [N3-R3][N3-R5]. This points to a broader problem: even when instrumentation exists, it may not be sufficient to resolve the full range of relevant signals.

The explicit FEM study for friction drilling explicitly uses adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence, which suggests that the process is computationally intensive and may require specialized monitoring approaches [N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that inverse methods are used to match measured and modeled thrust force, but this also implies that the data required for inverse calibration may be incomplete or noisy [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. In-process monitoring is further constrained by the need for both high temporal resolution and spatial resolution, which current instrumentation often struggles to provide [N1-R3][N1-R5][N5-F4].

## 4) Material property changes under severe plastic deformation complicate interpretation
Severe plastic deformation in friction drilling alters material properties through work hardening and microstructural evolution. The friction drilling dissertation states that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature, and that details of these changes are difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5]. The same source also links the process to microstructural alterations associated with friction drilling of steel, aluminum, and titanium [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This indicates that friction drilling is a form of severe plastic deformation that can induce significant microstructural transformation, even though the exact nature of those transformations may remain poorly resolved in experimental observation [N3-R5].

Work hardening and microstructural evolution are the primary mechanisms by which material properties change. The gradation extrusion study on severe plastic deformation reports that work hardening and grain refinement during local severe plastic deformation led to a considerable increase in hardness [N2-R1]. It also states that large incremental deformation by too many forming elements may result in locally heterogeneous microstructures and failure near the billet surface caused by localization of deformation [N2-F1]. This is directly relevant to friction drilling because the process also involves localized severe plastic deformation and can produce heterogeneous microstructures. The evidence further supports the conclusion that friction drilling can produce a gradient in material properties and microstructure rather than uniform strengthening [N2-R1][N2-F1].

## 5) Tool-workpiece contact and heat/pressure effects alter deformation behavior
Friction drilling is fundamentally a contact-based process where tool-workpiece interaction generates both heat and pressure. The process relies on the heat generated from the frictional force between the tool and sheet metal workpiece to soften, penetrate, and deform the workpiece [N3-R2][N3-R5]. Tool wear mechanisms are categorized into abrasive wear, adhesive wear, and oxidative wear [N3-R1]. These contact effects are not passive; they actively shape the deformation path by changing the frictional resistance and the heat generation profile during drilling.

The frictional heating and contact pressure in friction drilling are directly tied to the thermomechanical response of the material. The explicit finite element method (FEM) used in friction drilling modeling accounts for large plastic strain, large plastic deformation, and high-temperature work-material deformation, with adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence [N4-F3]. This highlights that the process simultaneously generates high temperatures and localized plastic deformation, and that the resulting thermomechanical state cannot be separated from the contact mechanics. The study also reports that the peak temperature of the workpiece approaches the work-material solidus temperature [N4-F3], underscoring the extreme thermal conditions that can arise during friction drilling.

Tool wear and heat generation together alter material deformation behavior. Tool wear mechanisms—abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative—change how the tool interacts with the workpiece, affecting the force transmission, friction coefficient, and hence the localized heating and plastic deformation [N3-R1]. The inverse method used in thermo-mechanical finite element modeling of friction drilling matches measured and modeled thrust force to determine a coefficient of friction of 0.7 in that study [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. This implies that wear-induced changes in friction behavior are not just experimental artifacts; they are meaningful deformation drivers that must be incorporated into process analysis. The model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy [N4-F3], showing that friction drilling is a highly coupled thermomechanical process where contact effects are central to the deformation response.

## 6) Material removal or softening can distort property determination
Material removal or softening further complicates property determination. The friction drilling process is described as relying on heat generation to soften the workpiece and allow penetration and deformation [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This means that the material is not simply being cut in the traditional sense; it is being softened locally, which can lead to non-uniform deformation behavior and make it difficult to separate true material response from process-induced softening.

The tool-workpiece interaction also generates localized subsurface effects, as friction drilling changes workpiece microstructure and material properties due to high strain and temperature [N3-R3][N3-R5]. Because the material is being softened and deformed by localized heating and friction, the measured properties may reflect a mixture of the intrinsic material behavior and the process-induced state, making direct determination of the material’s intrinsic physical properties challenging [N3-R3][N3-R5].

## 7) Residual stresses and localized deformation affect property uniformity
Residual stresses and localized deformation affect property uniformity. The friction drilling dissertation notes that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature [N3-R3][N3-R5], and that tool wear mechanisms are categorized into abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative wear [N3-R1]. These effects are likely to produce localized changes in the deformation state and residual stress state.

The residual stress literature cited here also states that local friction conditions are the primary cause of substantial surface residual stress [N6-R2], and that residual stresses resulting from thermo-mechanical processing can cause in-process cracking, machining distortion, in-service distortion, and/or cracking [N6-R4]. This means that friction drilling does not just change the bulk material; it can also generate significant residual stress fields that alter the mechanical response and uniformity of the material.

## 8) Surface and bulk property behavior can differ significantly
The difference between bulk and surface property behavior is especially important in friction drilling. The process relies on heat generation to soften, penetrate, and deform the workpiece [N3-R2][N3-R5], which suggests that surface and subsurface layers may experience different deformation histories, temperatures, and strain rates compared to the bulk. The subsurface microstructure evolution and residual stress literature explicitly investigates the effect of cutting on microstructure and subsurface properties of a cut specimen [N6-R5]. This is directly relevant because friction drilling can generate localized subsurface effects that are distinct from the bulk material.

The evidence also indicates that work hardening and grain refinement can produce a considerable increase in hardness [N2-R1], while localized deformation can lead to heterogeneous microstructures and failure near the billet surface [N2-F1]. Together, these findings show that friction drilling can produce a surface-dominated strengthening response alongside a bulk-dominated deformation response, with the subsurface acting as an intermediate layer where residual stresses and microstructural gradients accumulate [N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R5].

## 9) Modeling and data integration are limited by gaps and calibration dependence
The main gaps between experimental data and predictive models are the mismatch between observed process behavior and the assumptions embedded in the model. The thermo-mechanical finite element modeling study explicitly states that the model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements with reasonable accuracy [N4-F3]. This is a strong validation statement, but it also implies a gap: the model captures some observable quantities well, yet it still requires inverse methods to estimate parameters such as the coefficient of friction [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. This gap suggests that experimental data are not sufficient on their own to fully parameterize the model, and that model predictions depend on calibration against limited process outputs.

A major need for data fusion or multi-scale modeling arises because friction drilling involves both macroscopic and microscopic effects. The process is described as producing large plastic strain, large plastic deformation, and high-temperature work-material deformation, and the explicit FEM study uses adaptive meshing, element deletion, and mass scaling to enable convergence [N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that microstructure evolution and residual stress are important outcomes of the process [N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R3]. This means that a single-scale model may miss the coupling between macroscopic thermomechanical behavior and microscopic microstructural evolution. The cited friction drilling dissertation also reports that workpiece microstructure and material properties change due to high strain and temperature, yet details of these changes are difficult to capture experimentally [N3-R3][N3-R5]. This suggests a clear need for multi-scale modeling that integrates process-level thermomechanical analysis with microstructure evolution and residual stress prediction [N4-F3][N3-R3][N6-R3].

Limitations of inverse methods and calibration are evident in the friction drilling literature. The inverse method used in thermo-mechanical finite element modeling determines a coefficient of friction of 0.7 by matching measured and modeled thrust force [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. While this is a useful calibration approach, it also shows that the inverse method depends heavily on the quality and representativeness of the experimental data. If the measured signals are incomplete, noisy, or biased by process effects such as tool wear or localized softening, the resulting calibration may not generalize well [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The same study also reports that the model is validated by comparing thrust force, torque, and temperature to experimental measurements, but the evidence does not indicate whether all relevant process variables are captured [N4-F3]. This implies a calibration limitation: the model may be tuned to some observable outputs, but it may still underpredict or misrepresent other important quantities.

The cited constant strain rate nanoindentation study reinforces the broader limitation of inverse methods in high-strain-rate processes. It shows that impact-based methods produce variable strain rates with depth, making it difficult to extract representative material properties [N5-F4]. This is directly relevant to friction drilling, where the process is itself a high-strain-rate, high-temperature deformation event and where the measured output may reflect a mixture of material response and process-induced softening [N3-R3][N3-R5]. In that context, inverse methods may become overly dependent on the selected calibration targets and may fail to account for the true underlying deformation mechanism.

## 10) Overall conclusion
The main challenges of determining the physical properties of materials during severe plastic deformation in friction drilling are therefore:

- **Measurement difficulty**: Transient, localized, and coupled signals are hard to capture in real time.
- **Sensor limitations**: Strain rate and temperature affect sensor accuracy and response; high-frequency sampling is needed, but current instrumentation may still be inadequate.
- **In-process monitoring limits**: Even when instrumentation exists, it may not resolve the full range of relevant signals.
- **Material property changes**: Work hardening, microstructural evolution, and residual stresses alter the material state.
- **Localized and surface-bulk mismatch**: Surface and subsurface properties often differ from the bulk, and residual stress fields can reduce uniformity.
- **Tool-contact effects**: Friction, heat, pressure, and tool wear actively shape the deformation response.
- **Modeling and calibration gaps**: Experimental data do not fully parameterize predictive models, and inverse methods depend heavily on calibration quality.

Taken together, these challenges mean that determining the true physical properties of materials during friction drilling is not straightforward. The process itself is a highly coupled thermomechanical event in which measurement, deformation, and modeling are tightly intertwined, and accurate property determination requires both better instrumentation and more comprehensive integration of process, microstructure, and residual stress data [N3-R3][N3-R5][N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N5-F4][N6-R2][N6-R4].
